title: Runtime evolution strategy: LTS divergence policy and upgrade mitigations
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: define an actionable semantic versioning policy and LTS divergence rules for the serving runtime, and deliver upgrade mitigations (automation + shims + rollout gates) so customers can adopt new major/minor releases with minimal disruption. This ticket captures the runtime policy, classification of change types, required signals for rollout gates, and the initial set of tooling we will deliver as part of runtime-2.0 launch.

Policy summary (high level):
- MAJOR (X.y.z): any change that can break existing clients or client adapters (API surface changes, wire format alteration, removal of an endpoint or RPC, incompatible behavior changes to inference semantics) requires a MAJOR bump. Major changes must be behind explicit opt-in, have migration guides, and be gated by extended canaries + client-side adapters.
- MINOR (x.Y.z): additive features and non-breaking API extensions (new optional fields, new model routing hints, additional metrics) use MINOR. MINOR releases are allowed on both main and LTS channels but only when compatibility tests pass against LTS client contracts.
- PATCH (x.y.Z): bug fixes, performance improvements, and backward-compatible internal refactors go in PATCH. PATCH releases may be cherry-picked to active LTS branches following the LTS cherry-pick policy.

LTS channel model:
- We maintain two LTS channels: active-lts (12 months from branch point) and maintenance-lts (additional 12 months for security/critical fixes). LTS branches only accept PATCHes and explicitly approved MINORs that have been verified by compatibility automation and signed off by the runtime stewardship group. MAJOR changes are not merged into LTS.
- Divergence policy: if a MINOR feature is needed by an LTS customer, we require either (1) a compatibility shim that preserves old contract, (2) a documented opt-in feature flag on the LTS branch, or (3) a backported compatibility test ensuring no behavior regression. The default is to avoid divergence: prefer adapters or client-side SDKs to deal with new behavior.

Rollout gates and signals (must be checked before progressing release stage):
1) Unit + integration compatibility matrix: 95% of our public SDK adapters must pass a compatibility suite that validates request/response shapes, error codes, and KV cache semantics.
2) Telemetry safety thresholds: error rate delta < 0.5% absolute and tail latency P99 increase < 10% compared to baseline in canary.
3) Consumer contract alerts: if we see any customer using a deprecated field, notify them via usage report and generate an automatic migration ticket in Customer Success queue.
4) Gradual rollout windows: canary -> 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback on signal breach.
5) Manual sign-off gates: security, privacy, and enterprise compliance must explicitly approve MAJOR or opt-in MINOR changes for Dedicated/Private customers.

Upgrade tooling to ship alongside policy:
- compatibility-checker (CLI): runs a suite of contract tests against a local or remote runtime. Outputs a human-readable report and machine-parsable artifact used by CI.
- shim-generator: attempts to auto-generate input/output adapters for common breaking patterns (renamed fields, moved payloads). The generator will produce a candidate shim with tests and a PR template.
- migration-assistant: a hosted UI + CLI that scans a customer's API usage (via anonymized telemetry or customer-provided traces) and produces a prioritized list of affected call sites and recommended changes. For privacy-sensitive customers, this runs inside their VPC.
- deprecation headers and runtime warnings: runtime will emit structured deprecation warnings in X-Redwood-Warn headers and telemetry dimensions when deprecated features are invoked. Header format and retention policy are standardized.
- SDK compatibility helper: SDKs will include a compatibility shim layer that can opt into backward-compat behavior for a configured window (e.g., 90 days) to help customers migrate.

Tradeoffs considered:
- Strict semver with no LTS exceptions minimizes customer confusion but slows ability to ship iterative improvements to LTS customers. We chose a pragmatic approach: no MAJORs to LTS, selective MINOR backports when compatibility can be guaranteed.
- Auto-shims reduce migration friction but add maintenance burden and risk of subtle behavior drift; the shim-generator will be conservative and require human review for anything beyond trivial renames.

Operational and telemetry requirements:
- New compatibility telemetry events must be emitted in all releases and ingested into the rollout dashboard (console-telemetry). Event schema examples are linked below.
- Define SLIs for migration success: % of affected customers who migrate within deprecation window, average time-to-migrate, number of rollback incidents.

Deliverables for this ticket:
- Final policy document (this ticket links to the Confluence page).
- compatibility-checker v1 (CLI + CI integration).
- shim-generator prototype and two example shims for common rename and enum-extension scenarios.
- Release gates added to our rollout pipeline with telemetry thresholds implemented.
- Migration-assistant MVP integration plan for Private deployments.

Acceptance criteria (see field below for machine-readable list): runtime-2.0 release conforms to the above policy and new automation prevents accidental MAJOR-like behavior from reaching LTS branches.

Open questions:
- How do we treat behavioral changes that are technically backward-compatible but change model output distribution (e.g., new kernel optimizations affecting sampling)? Proposal: classify these as potentially 'compatibility-affecting' and require additional evaluation tests with our eval-sets.
- What is the eviction strategy for long-lived LTS branches that drift far from main (tooling or end-of-life cadence)? Proposal: a mandatory rebase/upgrade path every 12 months triggered by security or major platform shifts.
